runs.analysis: Candidate A is substantive and plan-specific, but it breaks the stage's format constraints. Bullets run about 200–450 words against a ~80-word limit. The same findings repeat across many reviews. It frames an elaborate "Version 1 vs Version 2" in Review 7. Some recommendations are unrealistic, such as setting up the maintenance trust fund legal structure by September 2026. Candidate B keeps bullets near the length limit, gives exactly three per question, and covers more distinct issues: UNCLOS classification, environmental oversight, climate recalibration, grid agreements, ownership transfer and the investor return-timeline mismatch. B has some numeric or logic slips: "3-8 billion maintenance liability annually", and the 2046/2051 dates. It also has less interaction analysis than A. Overall B fits the stage better, repeats itself less, and is more useful downstream.

Candidate A follows the stage format: exactly 3 bullets per question, roughly 80–130 words each, consistent length through Review 16, and dated, SMART-style recommendations. Candidate B ignores the ~80-word limit, with bullets of 200–700 words that grow worse in later reviews. It also adds invented or unnecessary named organizations (Arup, Mott MacDonald, McKinsey, Mercer, IBM, SAP) and a fabricated "Version 1" narrative, which the system prompt prohibits. B does have richer interdependency analysis and covers extra topics such as maritime traffic, workforce, and refinancing. Both repeat content across reviews and both have questionable revenue figures. A's concision, constraint compliance and actionability outweigh B's added depth.

Constraints: exactly three bullets of ~80 words, no snowballing, no invented history, figures consistent with the document.

A mostly keeps bullets compact (some ~100 words), and its figures come largely from the document (€1.3B holding cost, €4.32B FX exposure, 32.2 km² buildable area, 60% tenant trigger, Risks 2, 3, 5 and 7). Its actions name an owner and a date. Weaknesses: some unsupported numbers (€4B–€6B NPV loss, 5% EPC premium), speculative changed assumptions framed as "may have", a mild "Version 1" reference, and somewhat generic automation items.

B has many specific, quantified recommendations (liquidated damages, Phase 0 itemisation, contingency reserve). But its bullets run 120–180 words, which is the snowballing the instructions forbid. It fabricates "since Version 1" facts (mid-2024 baseline, post-2024 mandates, EDF reactor maintenance). It has odd or inconsistent dates and figures: Phase 1 FID at 2029-10-04 although Phase 1 runs in years 1–3, "€30–42B USD hardware spend" for Phases 1–2, Phase 1 hardware rising "beyond" a €5–10B Phase 1 budget, and Phase 2 CAPEX of €30–50B against the plan's €25–45B. It also invents specifics such as a biomass heat partner and a "Power Readiness Lockout Clause", and the heat-reuse arithmetic (€30B to €30.2B) is trivial.

B is more detailed but breaks format and length discipline and invents history. A follows the stage constraints more closely and is more consistent with the document.

Both candidates give 16 reviews with exactly three items each, and both draw on the same document themes: RTE grid timing, the unbudgeted 128.8 km² buffer holding cost, the DGSI/ANSSI sign-off, the 60% tenant trigger, and FX hedging.

A is more specific and decision-useful. It gives owners, dates and cost ranges. Examples are a Phase 0 hydrological study, ANSSI review started early with two alternative isolation architectures, and ROW easements decoupled from financing triggers. It also adds a contingency reserve and a split of the buffer into a permanent offset and an expansion reserve. It has three weaknesses:
- The bullets run about 120–180 words, well over the ~80-word limit.
- The FX numbers don't reconcile. Hedging 70% of €30–42B leaves roughly €9–12B unhedged, which doesn't match the stated "below €1B" or "€4.32B" residual.
- Review 10 frames changes "since Version 1 / mid-2024". The prompt warned against that, though A hedges it with "if".

B is closer to the length and format constraints and mostly stays within the document's figures. It adds useful points of its own: sequencing RTE fee submission after 30% LOIs, staging heavy civil works on a trained-supervisor cohort, a latency SLA in the LOIs, and Water Engineer and Technical Verifier roles. It is vaguer in many places ("unspecified upfront cost", "finalize immediately"). Its single-sentence bullets are dense and hard to read. Some KPIs are muddled, such as the "60% sovereign penetration" KPI, which conflates the tenant trigger with sovereign share. Its Review 10 is generic and not tied to the plan. It also has a typo ("E100B+").

A's depth and actionable detail outweigh its verbosity and its FX inconsistency, though not by much.

Both follow the 16-review, three-bullet structure and cover the same core issues (liability pivot, PRM timing, governance agility, float, royalty audit, T+5). Both exceed the ~80-word bullet limit and invent quantifications. A is somewhat tighter and names owners clearly, but it has an internal inconsistency (KPI 2 target 150% with an alert at 160%), overclaims ("years ahead of schedule"), has a muddled Review 13.2, invents figures such as "3-7% of annual operational budget", has a stray "**", and mostly gives vague timing ("Q1/Q2", "immediately"). B is more concrete and decision-useful, with explicit dates, thresholds (8% year one, 20% year three, 95% T+5), references to work-breakdown tasks, and specific mitigations and contingencies. B's weaknesses are longer bullets, heavy invented euro impacts, a KPI 3 range mismatch (150–250% versus 150–200%), and a Review 10 that wrongly assumes the project is already months underway (it treats provisional binding as overdue and cites 2026 grant utilization). That premise error affects roughly two bullets. On balance B is slightly more useful for downstream planning, though the margin is small.

Both candidates follow the 16-review structure with exactly three bullets each. Both also pick up the same main issues from the expert review: the liability pivot, accessibility timing, Fast-Track governance, float capitalization and cost-audit risk.

Candidate A is more specific and decision-useful. It gives concrete dates (TSC by 2026-06-14, V0.9 by 2026-11-14), measurable thresholds (8% in year one, T+5 on 95% of endpoints, 150% float trigger) and references to document artifacts (work breakdown task IDs, Risk and Decision numbers). Its recommendations are close to SMART.

A has real flaws:
- Review 10 treats "today" as 2026-10-04 and claims the month-6 milestone is already overdue. That contradicts the plan's stated date of 2026-05-14 and invents a problem.
- Review 10 also refers to "Q1–Q3 2026 grant utilization" and "six-month implementation progress", which are not grounded in the document.
- Several figures look invented or inconsistent: EUR 5–10M daily settlement losses, EUR 50–75M annual fines, and a KPI that states 150–250% and 150–200% for the same reserve.
- Bullets run well over the roughly 80-word target, and the EUR 5–10M daily losses figure is applied heavily across reviews.

Candidate B stays closer to the length discipline and ties actions to the plan's named roles (Liaison Manager, Regulatory Economist, Conformance Testing Coordinator, and others). It has no major date contradiction. It is weaker on specificity:
- Deadlines like "by Q2" or "by end of Q1" are ambiguous given the May 2026 start.
- Some claims are unrealistic or unsupported: achieving the 40% target "years ahead of schedule", a "100% ROI loss", and a "50% failure" to meet the modal-shift target.
- Several items are speculative, such as the 2% (€30M) behavioral study and the €20–40M CAPEX figure.
- Review 7 is generic.
- Review 16 has a stray "**".
- Review 2 mixes positives and negatives loosely.

Overall, A offers more actionable, quantified and timed guidance despite its date error and invented numbers. B is more compliant on length but vaguer and less SMART. I give A a slight edge.

Candidate A: Its dates mostly fall after the 2026-05-03 start, and it assigns actions to named roles. Its showstopper risks are distinct and relevant: the health-data MOU, cooling-center engineering failure, and CRM failure with a fallback plan. It repeats the MCR theme less than B and covers more topics. Weaknesses: many bullets run well over ~80 words, some figures look invented (€400k/yr, 25% service reduction), the "mid-March" readiness assumption is odd, and Review 7 uses a "Version 1/2" framing.

Candidate B: Its figures are often specific and mostly consistent, and its sequencing logic is good. However, it repeats the MCR/€1.5M gate theme in six of the sixteen reviews, which violates the "no repeats" instruction. Several recommended deadlines are before or on the project start date (2026-04-15, 04-28, 05-01, and a market survey "by 05-03"), so they are stale or impossible. It mentions "Brussels and Paris case studies", which looks invented. It has an arithmetic error: 30→10 minutes over 1,000 units saves ~333 hours, not 167. Many bullets are far over the ~80-word target.

Overall, A is somewhat more actionable and less repetitive, so A wins narrowly.

I could not see the source documents, so I judged both candidates on internal consistency, specificity and how well they follow the stage's constraints.

Candidate A has concrete owners, dates, quantities and costs in almost every bullet. Examples: MCR segregation memo by 05-07, a contractor survey with binding quotes before POs, an audit of 10 Tier 1 sites by 05-10, a baseline data pull by 05-15, and a cost-overage impact calculation. Its recommendations are close to SMART, and the Timeline Dependencies and Budget Clarifications sections are logically sequenced and actionable. Its weaknesses are real. Bullets often run well over the ~80-word limit. Review 7 invents "Brussels and Paris case studies" and a Version 1/Version 2 narrative. Several recommended deadlines (04-15, 04-28, 05-01) have already passed or are same-day relative to 2026-05-03. Some figures look loosely estimated (15–25% mortality, 167 hours saved).

Candidate B stays shorter and closer to the length limit and cites the plan's own structure (Decisions, Risks, Roles). Its content is more generic and vaguer, with fewer dates and thinner SMART quality. Examples: "100% penalty fees", "Reviewer 2 (Procurement)", "Risk 2.6.C", and unsupported percentages such as 40%, 50% and 25%. It also has logic problems. It recommends ring-fencing an extra €70k from the MCR while elsewhere stressing MCR lock-down. The Review 13 reasoning on procurement versus installation sequencing is muddled. Review 10 refers to mid-March and April timelines that are already past. Review 7 is bland. It does catch some useful points A misses: liability and indemnification for the triage script, volunteer and NGO insurance costs, and the CRM fallback. It also still has some invented-looking quantifications.

Overall, A is more decision-useful and specific, though it has length and invention violations. B is tidier but vaguer and has some odd reasoning. I give A a slight edge.
